components.text: The move identifies the unsupported leap from first-person self-authentication to universally normative logic and mathematics.
The inference from self-authenticating existence to universally normative logical and mathematical principles.
It asks for the principle connecting claims about an individual’s thinking to truth in all possible worlds.
It also challenges the extension from first-person epistemic certainty to universally necessary propositions.
The unexpressed principle connecting claims about belief and actual reality to necessity across every possible world.
The extension from an individual thinker’s certainty to a universally applicable necessary principle.
It replaces the demand for an externally existing proposition with a distinction between objective reality and mind-dependent sentences.
Whether a necessarily true proposition must exist independently as an entity beyond the reality it describes.
It supplies invariant reality-identity, including temporal scope, as the requested connective principle.
The requested basis for extending identity beyond present thought to temporal and modal necessity.
It argues that the assertion that reality remains reality already relies on an invariant law of identity.
It contests the denial of antecedent presuppositions by identifying identity and linguistic intelligibility used in the argument.
It asserts that identity is an objective, mind-independent mental entity rather than merely a sentence.
The claim that direct experience precedes and requires no invariant logical or linguistic conditions.
The use of invariant identity while denying antecedent logical presuppositions.
The status of logic as more than a contingent human sentence.
It answers that logic, mathematics, and language are derived after experience rather than assumed as foundational justificatory premises.
Whether logic, mathematics, and language are antecedent justificatory presuppositions or later conclusions from experience.
It offers God’s reality and self-revelation as the framework authorizing logical, mathematical, moral, and interpersonal presuppositions.
It provides the Christian framework as a contrary account of the antecedent conditions of intelligibility.
The proposed experiential foundation for logic, mathematics, language, morality, and interpersonal intelligibility.
The claim that God is unnecessary for the preconditions of intelligibility.
It argues that necessarily obtaining immaterial truths are mental objects requiring a mind, not merely contingent sentences.
It rejects treating necessary truths as wholly human-created products derived after experience.
Whether necessary logical and mathematical truths are merely human sentences or mind-dependent objects requiring a mind.
Whether human construction exhausts the status of logical and mathematical truth.
It identifies the conflation between objective relations and human descriptive languages as the failure in the mind-requirement inference.
It denies that objective objects and relations require the Christian framework for their existence.
The inference from necessary relations and truths to their existence as mental objects in an absolute divine mind.
The claim that objective intelligibility requires the Christian divine framework.
It identifies an equivocation between contingent linguistic expressions and the necessary truths those expressions purport to describe.
It rejects the tree-word analogy as inadequate for necessarily true logical and mathematical content.
The conflation of contingent human linguistic systems with the necessary truths or relations those systems express.
The analogy between ordinary contingent words and logical identity statements.
It argues that necessary conceptual descriptions do not thereby sustain the physical objects they describe.
It challenges the claim that a mind is required for physical particles to continue existing.
The inference that a divine or conceptual mind is required for physical entities to remain existent.
The claimed explanatory dependence of physical intelligibility upon God’s mind.
The treatment of conceptual truth as ontologically sustaining what it describes.
It relocates the persistence explanation from God’s nature directly to reality’s nature, preserving the demand for a stopping point.
It denies that a separate divine mind is required to terminate the explanatory regress.
It argues that necessary descriptions do not add a separate sustaining entity.
Whether persistence needs an external divine ground rather than being explained by the nature of reality itself.
Whether assigning necessary explanatory status to God improves upon assigning it directly to reality.
It blocks the parity argument by distinguishing necessary uncreated God from the created cosmos.
The symmetry claim that whatever explains God’s persistence by nature can be transferred directly to created reality.
The assumption that divine and physical persistence may be evaluated under the same ontological category.
It answers the parity argument by assigning necessity to God and contingency to created reality.
It maintains that evidential reasoning presupposes immaterial conditions of intelligibility grounded in the Christian worldview.
It contends that materialism lacks a ground for the immaterial necessary truths used in description.
The claim that reality can receive the same nature-based persistence explanation as God without contradiction or loss.
The denial that created material reality requires any external ground or sustainer.
The proposal that objective relations need no divine ground.
It reiterates indubitable existence of a potentially mistaken thinker as the sufficient non-theistic epistemic starting point.
It affirms the original self-validating premise but does not answer the objection concerning universal logical scope.
It supplies no connective principle between self-certainty and truth in all possible worlds.
The asserted distinction between necessary God and contingent creation as a ground for the preconditions of intelligibility.
The missing bridge from undeniable first-person existence to the full conditions of intelligibility.
The requested principle linking self-certainty to universal and modal conclusions.
